title: India's Central Bank Just Ordered a Kill Switch on Every AI System in Banking
excerpt: The RBI's draft framework demands board-level oversight, mandatory human alternatives for customers, and the ability to shut down any AI model on command — the most prescriptive rules of their kind anywhere.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India has proposed what may be the world's most detailed regulatory framework for artificial intelligence in banking — and its centrepiece is a mechanism that sounds borrowed from science fiction: a mandatory kill switch for every AI model deployed by a financial institution.

The draft *Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026*, released on June 24, applies to commercial banks, small finance banks, NBFCs, payment banks, cooperative banks, regional rural banks, asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies. In other words, virtually every entity that touches Indian retail finance.

## What the Rules Demand

The framework requires regulated entities to build mechanisms that can override, suspend, or completely deactivate any AI model — instantly, on command. Banks must establish what the RBI calls "human-in-the-loop arrangements," including explicit kill-switch capabilities, override features, and periodic human review of AI-generated decisions.

For customer-facing AI systems — the chatbots, virtual assistants, and recommendation engines that millions of account holders interact with daily — the rules go further. Banks must disclose when customers are interacting with an AI system, communicate its limitations, and provide an option to switch to a human representative at any time. Generative AI systems that interface with customers must also be protected against prompt injection attacks and adversarial inputs.

Third-party AI models, including those from global technology vendors, receive no exemptions. Banks remain fully accountable for outcomes generated by external AI systems. Every third-party model must undergo independent validation before deployment, and institutions must secure audit rights for both themselves and the RBI.

## Why NRIs Should Care

The guidelines matter well beyond Mint Street. Millions of non-resident Indians hold NRE and NRO accounts, invest through Indian brokerage platforms, send remittances via UPI, and interact with bank chatbots that increasingly make credit, pricing, and risk decisions. If an AI model at an Indian bank goes rogue — mispricing a fixed deposit, erroneously flagging a cross-border transaction as fraudulent, or drifting on credit scoring in a way that disadvantages NRI applicants — the RBI now wants a red button that shuts it down before the damage compounds.

The framework also mandates board-level oversight. Every institution must establish a board-approved Model Risk Management Framework covering governance, classification, validation, deployment, monitoring, and decommissioning. Decommissioned models must remain documented for at least ten years.

## A Global Benchmark

The RBI's approach is arguably more prescriptive than what Western regulators have attempted. The EU AI Act takes a risk-based approach but does not mandate kill switches or customer-facing transparency at this level of specificity. The Federal Reserve has issued general guidance on model risk but nothing comparable in scope for AI-specific systems. India's framework sits closer to what the Bank of England has hinted at — but the RBI appears to have got there first.

Industry reaction has been cautiously positive. "The guidance removes the bigger blocker: uncertainty," said Ajay Sirikonda, Partner and Leader for Financial Services Risk Management at EY India. "Banks have sat on AI not just because it was costly, but because no one had said what was allowed."

The draft is open for public consultation until July 24. Once finalised, it will replace the RBI's existing 2002 guidance on credit risk models — a framework drafted in an era when the most advanced model in Indian banking was a spreadsheet.
